endorsements.quote: Pre-market evidence requirements should continue to be tiered based on risk classification.
There is a need for periodic but consistent performance monitoring with predefined intervention thresholds, and many of these technologies should include PCCPs.

Importantly, validation must extend beyond single-institution datasets to include diverse patient populations and clinical environments to ensure generalizability and mitigating risks of algorithmic bias [ 61 , 62 ].
Post-market evidence generation and additional data collection should also be mandatory for all these technologies [ 40 ], with reporting requirements that scale with risk level.

These technologies should require more comprehensive pre-market evaluation, including clinical validation studies, human factors assessment, analysis of learning curves, and algorithmic bias evaluation.
Standards should include automated reporting mechanisms, error logging, standardized incident classification systems, and clear escalation procedures when performance thresholds are not met [ 60 ].

unlisted_practices: Regulators should adopt a three-tier risk-stratified classification (low, moderate, high) for digital surgery technologies aligned with existing FDA pathways.
Regulators should require evidence of safe integration within existing surgical workflows for moderate-risk digital surgery technologies.
Regulators should require rigorous randomized clinical trials with hybrid effectiveness-implementation designs for high-risk digital surgery technologies.
Evaluators should validate AI surgical tools against clinically meaningful outcomes, not only technical metrics such as sensitivity and specificity.
Regulators should use pragmatic trial designs, adaptive study protocols, and long-term outcome tracking beyond traditional randomized controlled trials.

Developers should progress digital surgery technologies through the IDEAL framework stages and use stage-specific reporting guidelines such as DECIDE-AI, TRIPOD-AI, STARD-AI, SPIRIT-AI, and CONSORT-AI.
Professional societies and FDA-recognized collaborative communities should define consensus clinically relevant performance metrics and evaluation standards for surgical AI.
Regulators should adapt the CORE-MD clinical risk score to determine evidence requirements proportionate to risk for digital surgery technologies.
Regulators should require mandatory user training and competency verification for digital surgery technologies.
High-risk digital surgery systems should include failure/error detection, automatic fallback systems, and automatic shutdown triggers.
Regulators should require mandatory registry participation for high-risk digital surgery technologies.
Regulators should establish comprehensive cybersecurity standards tailored to real-time intraoperative surgical systems.
Regulators should clarify liability and responsibilities among device manufacturers and software developers for performance, safety monitoring, and adverse event reporting.
Evaluators should incorporate surgeon trust and usability as performance indicators.
Developers should define standardized, modality-specific technical metrics such as registration accuracy, latency thresholds, and fail-safe detection.
Regulators should include mandatory post-market surveillance even for low-risk digital surgery technologies.
